International Business Machines (IBM) stock returned -17.6%, dividends included, in the year to Monday, November 23. The S&P 500 returned 12%. Yet the business grew. Revenue rose 6.8% in the four quarters to September 2026. The operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 18.3% from 17.7% a year earlier.
Management did not blame an outside cause. On its October 21 call, it spoke of “strength across our portfolio and solid execution”. A short seller, someone who bets a stock will keep falling, would still push on three points. Rivals grow faster, IBM’s growth has been uneven, and its debt is heavier than the market’s.
Are IBM’s rivals growing faster?
Yes, three of the four peers we compare grew faster. Alphabet grew revenue 22.2% and Microsoft grew 17.9%. Amazon.com grew 15.4%. Only Accenture grew about as slowly as IBM, at 6.5%. Each company is measured over its own latest four quarters.
IBM stock lost 17.6% in a year, dividends included, even as its revenue grew 6.8%. If IBM is a large part of your savings and you live on its dividend, that is a long fall to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.
Slow sales growth is not a long-running problem at IBM. Yearly growth rose from 1.1% in the four quarters to September 2023 to 6.8% now. The quarters were uneven, though. Revenue grew 12.2% in the quarter to December 2025 and 9.5% in the quarter to March 2026. It then grew 1.1% in the quarter to June and 4.7% in the quarter to September.
What did IBM’s managers say about the uneven quarters?
Management named its own cause for the soft June quarter. “Last quarter, it impacted our software growth by 4-5 points when we were down double-digit transactional,” a manager said.
Transaction processing (TP) software then grew 10% in the September quarter. “I do not expect double-digit performance in TP to keep going,” a manager said candidly. Management also said about a quarter of the software speed-up came from deals that slipped from earlier quarters. So part of the September bounce was timing.
Does the cash show strain for an owner?
The payout does not. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment, was $14 billion over four quarters. Dividends took $6.3 billion and buybacks about $1 billion.
Debt is the softer spot. It stood at $67.1 billion, up from $59 billion five years earlier. That equals 30.5% of IBM’s market value, against 20.2% for the S&P 500.

The stock is cheaper while profit rose. At Monday’s close, IBM traded at 19.7 times its past year’s earnings, below 21.2 times for the S&P 500. At the end of September 2025, it traded at 33.3 times. Many shoppers look forward to Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of scoring a good deal or two. Adobe forecasts that consumers will spend over $15 billion online on Cyber Monday and $12.9 billion on Black Friday, making them two of the biggest shopping days of the year.
However, for some shoppers, these holidays can cost them more than they bargained for. A separate study from McAfee found a 91% year-over-year spike in the number of Americans reporting holiday shopping scams, and 60% of those who lost money lost at least $100.
"Black Friday and Cyber Monday create a perfect environment for scammers because consumers are actively looking for deals and often make quick purchasing decisions," said Michael Bruemmer, vice president of global data breach resolution and consumer protection at Experian.
Read more: 7 common banking scams (and how to avoid becoming a victim)
3 common holiday shopping scams and how to avoid them
Holiday shopping scams can take on many forms and be easy to miss. Shoppers rushing to get their holiday shopping done at the lowest possible prices may be less likely to notice a scam or vet purchases as carefully as they normally would.
Some of the most common holiday shopping scams include:
Phishing emails and text messages
Shoppers may receive fake text messages or emails from scammers posing as retailers or shipping companies.
"Phishing emails and text messages will always be a popular tactic for fraudsters, and the messages may appear to come from well-known retailers, shipping companies, or payment providers and are often designed to steal login credentials or financial information," said Bruemmer.
Legitimate retailers and shipping companies will never ask shoppers to share personal information via email or text. If you receive a text message or email that you suspect could be a phishing scheme, you can report this scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Gift card scams
Gift card scams occur year-round, but they tend to ramp up during the holiday season. Scammers may try to sell gift cards online at a "discount" and never send them, or sell cards whose balances have already been drained. Some scammers may even photograph gift cards in stores and wait for someone to purchase and load the card, then drain the balance.
When making any gift card purchases this holiday season, only purchase cards from trusted retailers or directly on the retailer's website rather than via a third-party website.
Fake online stores
Scammers may build fake websites that imitate trusted retailers to trick consumers into sharing their personal information. These websites can look quite convincing, but there are a few red flags to watch for that can help shoppers determine whether a website is legitimate.
This includes mobile apps or websites that ask shoppers to grant access to your contacts, text messages, stored passwords, or payment information. Other signs, such as misspelled words on the website or in the URL, discounts that are too good to be true, and limited or missing contact information, can also indicate that a website is fraudulent.
Shoppers can rely on tools such as Scamwise, ScamAdviser, and Google Safe Browsing to check whether a website is suspicious and receive alerts before visiting a fraudulent site.

This was all before tackling Sunday’s 26.2 miles with the boat balanced over his head.
And yes, the canoe made it through the entire race without ever touching water.
“Coming from Minnesota, I can't just throw a boat in an overhead compartment," Meier told Runner's World. "It was a logistical nightmare: where to keep it, where to sneak it into the race, and how people would react to it."
Despite the travel headaches, Meier came away from Philadelphia with his second personal record in as many weeks. It was another step in his latest undertaking: 52 marathons in 52 weeks, each while carrying a canoe, to raise awareness about protecting the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in northern Minnesota.
Meier, who manages a distillery when he isn't hauling boats around, wasn't exactly a seasoned runner when all this started. His introduction to the sport came through the Red Bull Urban Portage, an event that involved carrying a boat through downtown Minneapolis before paddling along the Mississippi River.
“I was really bad at paddling, but I could outrun people,” he recalled. Before the event, he bought a Northstar ADK canoe off Craigslist with every intention of selling it once the race was over. Instead, it found a home on his garage wall and managed to stick around for another year. Eventually, he started entering more races with it.
That eventually brought him to Minnesota's Ely Marathon in 2023, where he completed his first-ever 26.2-mile race while carrying a canoe. Since then, he's run only one conventional marathon without a boat, and what started solely as a personal experiment gradually became an opportunity to draw attention to a place he'd loved for years.
The Boundary Waters, a wilderness area known for its lakes, forests, and extensive canoe routes, has been at the center of a contentious debate over proposed mining operations. Think this year's been a big one for data centers and their relentless power demands? Wait until you get a load of 2028.
A new report from Goldman Sachs Research estimates that the US will add about 52 gigawatts of data center power capacity in 2028 — nearly triple the 18 gigawatts expected this year and more than five times last year's additions. That's after data center power capacity and demand grew nearly 30% year over year so far in 2026, with data centers accounting for more than a third of all US power demand growth.
The forecast suggests that many of the issues associated with the AI boom — from rising electricity bills to competition for power and growing community opposition to data centers — could get considerably worse before the decade is out.
It's not just that tech companies are building more data centers. They're building bigger and more power-hungry ones. Goldman expects the average power capacity of a US data center building to reach 49 megawatts in 2028, up from 31 this year and 16 in 2020. The growth is also expected to be highly concentrated geographically. Virginia and Texas alone are projected to account for 36% of new US data center power capacity in 2028.
The projected growth in 2028 far exceeds the assumptions underpinning Goldman's existing natural gas outlook, which anticipates average annual data center power capacity additions of 28 gigawatts from 2027 through 2035. The analysts said the new estimates reinforced their bullish outlook for US natural gas prices through 2030.
But that growth isn't guaranteed. While Goldman's estimates already account for historical rates of project delays and cancellations, roughly half of the data center power capacity expected to come online in 2028 isn't yet under construction. The analysts warned that political changes following the midterm elections, as well as growing local opposition to data centers, could lead to more project delays and cancellations than expected.
In other words, the AI industry's appetite for power is growing just as political tolerance for that appetite is being tested.

Corporate Bonds vs. Dividend Stocks: Which Pays a Retiree More Reliably?
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Investment-grade corporate bonds are paying their highest yields in a year. Moody’s Seasoned Baa Corporate Bond Yield, a benchmark for the lowest tier of investment-grade debt, stood at 6.59%[1] in its October 1, 2026 monthly reading. That was the most recent figure available on November 25, 2026, and the 12-month high. For comparison, the 10-year Treasury yielded 4.92%[2] on November 23, 2026. Below, we line those rates up against two of the market’s most reliable dividend payers.
How a Corporate Bond Pays You and What Happens at Maturity
A corporate bond is a loan you make to a company. In return, the company promises a fixed interest payment, called the coupon, usually twice a year, and agrees to repay the bond’s face value on a set maturity date. The coupon is locked in when the bond is issued. The market yield changes every trading day, though, because the bond’s price moves.
When rates rise, existing bond prices fall; when rates drop, prices rise. A buyer today gets about the current market yield only by holding the bond to maturity, and only if the issuer pays in full. Some corporate bonds carry floating coupons that reset with short-term rates, so their income isn’t locked in.
Credit ratings from agencies like Moody’s and S&P measure the odds of getting paid, with investment grade running from the top AAA/Aaa tier down to BBB-/Baa3. Baa is the lowest rung before junk territory. The Baa series quoted above tracks bonds with maturities of 20 years and above[1]. Shorter bonds and higher-rated issuers generally yield less. Corporate bonds carry no FDIC insurance and no government guarantee, so if the issuer defaults, recovery depends on the company’s assets and where your bond ranks among its creditors. Even Treasuries, backed by the U.S. government, protect only principal and interest paid at maturity, and if you sell before then, the price can be lower than what you paid.
A bond fund works differently. It holds hundreds of bonds, never matures, and has a share price that moves with interest rates every day. Its monthly payout rises or falls as old bonds mature and the manager buys new ones at whatever rates the market offers. Individual bonds have their own version of that problem, called reinvestment risk. When a bond matures, or the issuer calls it early (which usually happens after rates fall), you have to reinvest at whatever rate is available then.
The Baa yield’s 12-month path shows both risks. It bottomed at 5.81%[1] in February 2026 and then rose to its October high. Rising yields meant falling prices for anyone who already owned those bonds.
Dividend Safety Comes First in a Coupon Comparison
Bonds and dividends trade safety against growth. A bond coupon is a contract: missing a payment is a default, and bondholders get paid before shareholders if a company runs into trouble. A dividend is a board decision that can be cut or suspended at any meeting, but a dividend can grow every year, while a fixed coupon never rises. That makes dividend safety the first thing to check, ahead of yield.

Analysts have long questioned why Berkshire Hathaway does not pay dividends to its own shareholders. Buffett has always been confident in his ability to put the company's capital to better use. He believes investing in businesses and other opportunities can generate better returns than distributing cash to shareholders. Even when he feels Berkshire cannot find attractive investment opportunities for its growing cash pile, he would rather return capital through share buybacks than dividends. In a 2018 interview with CNBC, Buffett explained his thinking: "Dividends have the implied promise that you keep paying them forever and not decrease them." He has also argued that repurchasing Berkshire's own shares can be more beneficial for shareholders.
In a 2023 report, The Wall Street Journal cited Todd Finkle, a professor of entrepreneurship at Gonzaga University and author of a book about Buffett's career. Finkle summed up Buffett's approach by saying, "That's what he loves: dividends and buybacks."
Finkle noted that Buffett has been particularly good at identifying businesses that can withstand different economic cycles while continuing to increase their dividends. These investments have helped grow the value of Berkshire's stock portfolio over time while bringing in cash that the company can use to support its businesses, make acquisitions, and buy back its own shares. For Buffett, dividends aren't "the secret sauce, but they're part of it," Finkle said. In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?
Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.
It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.
Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.
Here are some key points:
- The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.
- Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.
- The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%.
- Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%.
- Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against.

Missouri proposal would establish statewide child safety standards
Draft legislation would establish a uniform process for determining when children are unsafe and how authorities should intervene
Members of a child welfare task force established by Gov. Mike Kehoe gather on Nov. 5 to discuss draft legislation that would require child welfare workers, juvenile officers, judges and service providers to use a consistent child safety framework (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
A Missouri child welfare task force has submitted draft legislation to Gov. Mike Kehoe that would define child safety in state law and require child welfare workers, judges and juvenile officers to follow a uniform process for identifying threats and determining when and how to intervene.
Kehoe created the 18-member task force by executive order in August, less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative committee held a hearing examining foster care deaths, child placements and turnover among frontline Children’s Division staff.
The proposed legislation describes the safety framework as a “sequential decision-making process” to identify safety threats, evaluate children’s vulnerabilities, assess a caregiver’s ability to protect a child and determine appropriate responses. Those could include community-based services, more structured intensive in-home services, temporary placements with relatives or longer-term removal from home.
Missouri lawmakers press child welfare leaders on foster care deaths, staff turnover
It’s similar to the safety assessment already used by Children’s Division investigators, called Structured Decision Making. That safety assessment was developed by the division and the Office of State Courts Administrator based on a guide published by the American Bar Association.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, media director for the Department of Social Services, said that while SDM is already the basis of initial safety assessments, “the broader, ongoing goal is to embed the safety framework throughout all practice areas — including when a child is in alternative care.”
The goal is to ensure that the reasons a child is considered unsafe — and what must change before that child can return home — are clearly described as the case moves through the child welfare system.
The legislation would require the division to establish the safety framework in state regulations and coordinate with the Office of State Courts Administrator to create standard forms for court reports and social service plans, as well as any other “uniform tools for the identification and evaluation of child safety.” The division would also develop training materials for juvenile and family courts, guardians ad litem, parents’ attorneys, law enforcement, medical professionals and child welfare agencies.
The legislation builds on efforts by division leadership to standardize child welfare practices statewide. Task force members said during the group’s Nov. 10 meeting that they plan to move forward with some changes, including developing standard forms, while lawmakers consider the legislation next year. Watts said the division also plans to begin promulgating rules needed to implement the proposed legislation.
Republican state Rep. Melissa Schmidt of Eldridge, who chairs the task force, has said throughout the group’s meetings that a shared framework and definitions will provide relief to overwhelmed division workers.
